trial_name: SEPSISPAM — High versus low blood-pressure target in patients with septic shock (2014)
citation: Asfar P, Meziani F, Hamel JF, et al; SEPSISPAM Investigators. High versus low blood-pressure target in patients with septic shock. N Engl J Med. 2014;370(17):1583-1593.
one_liner: Targeting a higher MAP (80–85 mmHg) compared to a lower MAP (65–70 mmHg) in septic shock did not reduce 28-day mortality and increased atrial fibrillation, though it reduced renal replacement therapy in chronic hypertension.

pico.population: Adult ICU patients with septic shock requiring vasopressors after fluid resuscitation (n=776 analysed).
pico.intervention: High-target MAP strategy (80–85 mmHg) maintained for 5 days using vasopressors (primarily norepinephrine).
pico.comparison: Low-target MAP strategy (65–70 mmHg) maintained for 5 days using vasopressors (primarily norepinephrine).
pico.outcome: Primary: 28-day mortality. Key secondary: 90-day mortality, renal replacement therapy, organ-support-free days, and adverse events.

background.existing_knowledge: MAP targets in septic shock were largely consensus-driven (typically ≥65 mmHg) with wide practice variation. Higher targets were hypothesized to benefit chronic hypertension due to right-shifted renal autoregulation.
background.knowledge_gap: Uncertainty whether higher MAP targets protect organs or cause net harm due to increased catecholamine exposure.
background.hypothesis: Targeting a higher MAP (80–85 mmHg) vs a lower MAP (65–70 mmHg) during early septic shock reduces 28-day mortality, with potential effect modification by pre-existing chronic hypertension.

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre, parallel-group, open-label trial with prespecified subgroup stratification by chronic arterial hypertension.

inclusion: Adults with septic shock requiring vasopressors despite fluid resuscitation
Minimum fluid load of 30 mL/kg prior to inclusion
Enrolment within 6 hours of shock onset
exclusion: Lack of consent or guardianship/prisoner status

methods.intervention: High-target MAP strategy: vasopressors (primarily norepinephrine) titrated to maintain MAP 80–85 mmHg for up to 5 days, with protocolised decrement schedules.
methods.comparison: Low-target MAP strategy: vasopressors titrated to maintain MAP 65–70 mmHg for up to 5 days, otherwise identical co-interventions.
methods.blinding: Open-label bedside hemodynamic management; objective outcomes evaluated unblinded.
methods.sample_size_power: 800 patients planned to detect a 10% absolute mortality reduction (45% to 35%) with 80% power at alpha 0.05; Peto-Haybittle interim monitoring (P<0.001) at 200, 400, 600 patients.
secondary_outcomes: Survival at day 28 without organ support (vasopressors, mechanical ventilation, or RRT)
Prespecified serious adverse events (atrial fibrillation, myocardial infarction)

headline_bullets: No difference in 28-day mortality between high-target (36.6%) and low-target MAP (34.0%) groups (HR 1.07; 95% CI 0.84–1.38; P=0.57).
High-target MAP significantly increased newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation (6.7% vs 2.8%; P=0.02).
Patients with chronic hypertension in the high-target group had lower RRT rates (31.7% vs 42.2%; P=0.046; interaction P=0.02) and less creatinine doubling (38.9% vs 52.0%; P=0.02).

outcomes_table.outcome: Survival at day 28 without organ support
outcomes_table.note: Organ support: vasopressors, ventilation, or RRT

subgroup_table.subgroup: Doubling of plasma creatinine — Chronic arterial hypertension

safety: Newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation: 6.7% (high-target) vs 2.8% (low-target), P=0.02.
Any serious adverse event: 19.1% (high-target) vs 17.8% (low-target), P=0.64.
Down-titration of vasopressors due to adverse effects occurred in 14/388 (3.6%) high-target patients.

domains.notes: Central computer-based randomisation with concealment and stratification by chronic hypertension; balance achieved (chronic hypertension 43.0% vs 44.6%; SAPS II 56.1 ± 15.5 vs 57.2 ± 16.2).
Open-label bedside MAP titration creates scope for performance bias; primary endpoint (mortality) is objective.
798 randomised; 22 excluded post-randomisation (14 low-target, 8 high-target) for consent/legal status; 388 per group analysed (776 total) on ITT basis.
MAP targets not achieved in 64/388 (16.5%) high-target vs 40/388 (10.3%) low-target (P=0.01). Observed MAPs averaged 85–90 mmHg in high-target and 70–75 mmHg in low-target, narrowing contrast.
Well balanced: SOFA 10.7 ± 3.1 vs 10.8 ± 3.1; delay from vasopressor start to inclusion 3.5 ± 2.2 vs 3.6 ± 2.1 hours; norepinephrine day 1 median 0.58 vs 0.45 µg/kg/min.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate-to-strong with robust allocation concealment and objective endpoints, though open-label design and incomplete MAP target separation narrowed physiological contrast.

domains.notes: Typical high-severity adult ICU septic shock population (~74–79% mechanically ventilated, ~43–45% chronic hypertension), conducted across 29 French ICUs.
High applicability to modern high-income ICUs using norepinephrine-first resuscitation early in shock (<6 hours).

external_validity.verdict: External validity is good for contemporary ICUs utilizing norepinephrine-first strategies in early septic shock.

strengths: Large, pragmatic, multicenter RCT testing a routine hemodynamic intervention
Prespecified stratification for chronic arterial hypertension
Objective primary mortality endpoint with high follow-up completeness
Clear separation in vasopressor dose (norepinephrine day 1 median 0.58 vs 0.45 µg/kg/min) and duration (4.7 vs 3.7 days)
limitations: Open-label MAP titration with potential for co-intervention bias
Protocol non-adherence in 16.5% high-target and 10.3% low-target groups
Achieved MAP in low-target arm averaged 70–75 mmHg, above the nominal 65–70 mmHg target
Final sample size (776) slightly under planned 800; control mortality (34.0%) lower than assumed 45%

critical_appraisal.summary: Methodologically rigorous trial demonstrating no mortality difference overall, with increased atrial fibrillation from higher vasopressor doses, alongside a signal for reduced RRT in chronic hypertension.
strengths: Multicenter randomisation with prespecified subgroup stratification
Documented physiological separation in MAP and catecholamine exposure
weaknesses: Overtreatment of low-target arm relative to protocol target (achieved 70–75 mmHg)

sections.authors_conclusion: Targeting a mean arterial pressure of 80 to 85 mmHg as compared with 65 to 70 mmHg did not significantly reduce mortality at 28 days among patients with septic shock.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Default to a MAP target of 65–70 mmHg for general septic shock; consider selective targeting of 80–85 mmHg in chronic hypertension to protect renal function if arrhythmia risks permit.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients with early septic shock requiring vasopressors.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Higher MAP targets should never be used; chronic hypertension patients may benefit renally.
implementation_caveats: Higher MAP targets require more vasopressors (median 0.58 vs 0.45 µg/kg/min) and longer duration (4.7 vs 3.7 days).
Monitor closely for new-onset atrial fibrillation when escalating MAP targets.

controversies.notes: The reduction in RRT in chronic hypertension (31.7% vs 42.2%) must be balanced against a more than doubling of atrial fibrillation risk (6.7% vs 2.8%).
Low-target arm achieved MAPs of 70–75 mmHg rather than 65–70 mmHg, potentially diluting potential differences between groups.

context_related_trials.relation: Pilot RCT in vasodilatory shock comparing lower (60–65 mmHg) vs higher (75–80 mmHg) MAP targets, confirming feasibility and potential subgroup heterogeneity.
Evaluated permissive hypotension (MAP 60–65 mmHg) in older patients with vasodilatory shock, supporting lower vasopressor exposure strategies.

unresolved_questions: Optimal individualised MAP target titration based on dynamic autoregulation parameters rather than numerical blood pressure cutoffs.
Whether non-catecholamine vasopressors reduce the arrhythmia burden associated with higher MAP targets.

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Target MAP 65–70 mmHg as default in septic shock to minimise catecholamine toxicity and atrial fibrillation, but consider 80–85 mmHg in chronic hypertension to reduce renal replacement therapy.
